title: 📘 UNIT 6: MAJOR GLOBAL ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGES
notes: Global environmental changes are major changes in ecosystems and natural resources caused by human activities and environmental processes.

title: 🌍 6.1 PERSISTENT ENVIRONMENTAL CHANGES
notes:
Persistent environmental changes are long-term changes that continue to affect ecosystems, biodiversity and natural resources.

Major forms :-
🔹 Habitat fragmentation/destruction
🔹 Agricultural intensification
🔹 Overexploitation of resources
🔹 Invasive species

⭐ These changes can reduce biodiversity, degrade ecosystems and threaten human livelihoods.

title: 🏞️ 6.1.1 HABITAT DESTRUCTION AND FRAGMENTATION
notes:
Habitat :- the physical environmental conditions that allow a particular species to survive and reproduce.

Habitat destruction/loss occurs when suitable living areas are destroyed or changed.

🌍 Major cause :- human modification of landscapes.

Five ways humans modify habitats :-
1️⃣ Perforation
2️⃣ Dissection
3️⃣ Fragmentation
4️⃣ Shrinkage
5️⃣ Attrition

🌋 Natural causes include floods, volcanic eruptions, earthquakes and temperature changes.

title: 🧩 6.1.1.1 EFFECTS OF HABITAT LOSS
notes:
Habitat loss and fragmentation can cause :-

🐾 Reduced wildlife populations
🌿 Loss of biodiversity
🦋 Loss of breeding areas
🍃 Reduced food and shelter
🔗 Disruption of ecological relationships
⚠️ Increased risk of species extinction

⭐ Species may survive for a period in degraded habitats even when they can no longer reproduce.

title: ⏳ 6.1.1.2 EXTINCTION DEBT
notes:
Extinction debt :- the time between landscape change or habitat degradation and the eventual extinction of a species.

📌 A species may remain alive for some time after its habitat becomes unsuitable.

⭐ Habitat restoration requires continuous management, protection and reconstruction of damaged areas.

title: 🌾 6.1.2 AGRICULTURAL INTENSIFICATION
notes:
Agricultural intensification :- increasing agricultural output per unit of input such as land, labour, time, fertilizer, seed and water.

🌱 Common methods :-
🔹 High-yield crop varieties
🔹 Fertilizers
🔹 Pesticides
🔹 Herbicides
🔹 Heavy machinery
🔹 Irrigation

⭐ It can increase food production, especially where population pressure is high, but improper intensification can damage natural resources.

title: ⚠️ 6.1.2.1 NEGATIVE EFFECTS OF AGRICULTURAL INTENSIFICATION
notes:
Major environmental impacts :-

🌿 Loss of biodiversity :- monocropping reduces agricultural diversity.

🌱 Soil degradation :- excessive chemical fertilizers and intensive land use reduce soil quality.

🧪 Pesticide pollution :- pesticides can remain in soil, air and water and move through food chains.

💧 Water pollution :- fertilizer nutrients can leach into water bodies.

🌳 Ecosystem destruction :- expansion of farmland can destroy forests, wetlands and other ecosystems.

🚜 Soil compaction :- heavy machinery can compact soil.

🦠 Increased pests and diseases :- monocropping can increase vulnerability to pests and diseases.

title: 🌱 6.1.2.2 SUSTAINABLE AGRICULTURAL INTENSIFICATION
notes:
Sustainable intensification aims to increase agricultural production while protecting natural resources.

Important approaches :-
💧 Improve fertilizer and water-use efficiency.
🌱 Use improved plant and animal varieties.
🛡️ Apply integrated soil management.
🐛 Apply integrated pest management.
🌳 Promote agroforestry.
🌾 Maintain crop diversity.

⭐ Main goal :- balance increasing food demand with biodiversity and natural-resource conservation.

title: ⛏️ 6.1.3 OVEREXPLOITATION OF RESOURCES
notes:
Overexploitation :- harvesting natural resources faster than their ability to regenerate.

Examples :-
🐟 Overfishing
🐄 Overgrazing
🌳 Over-logging
💧 Over-drafting of groundwater
🌿 Excessive harvesting of wild plants
🦌 Excessive hunting
⛏️ Excessive mineral extraction
🛢️ Excessive oil exploitation

⚠️ Result :- rapid depletion of resources and possible economic or ecological extinction.

title: 🐟 6.1.3.1 TYPES OF OVEREXPLOITATION
notes:
🐟 Overfishing :- fish stocks are reduced below the level needed to support long-term maximum sustainable yield.

🐄 Overgrazing :- livestock graze land beyond its carrying capacity.

🌳 Over-logging :- forests are cut faster than they can be regenerated.

💧 Over-drafting :- groundwater is extracted faster than the recharge rate.

⛏️ Mineral overexploitation :- minerals are extracted intensively as technology allows deeper and easier extraction.

title: 🛢️ 6.1.3.2 RESOURCE DEPLETION AND ITS EFFECTS
notes:
Increasing exploitation of minerals and fossil fuels reduces available stocks.

🛢️ Oil is particularly important for :-
🔹 Manufacturing
🔹 Agriculture
🔹 Mining
🔹 Transportation

⚠️ Oil depletion can contribute to :-
💰 Higher living costs
📉 Reduced business activity
🚚 Transport uncertainty
🌍 Environmental pollution
🌡️ Climate change

♻️ Solutions :- reduce waste, reuse materials, recycle, improve manufacturing efficiency and increase renewable-energy use.

title: 🦠 6.1.4 INVASIVE ALIEN SPECIES
notes:
Invasive alien species :- non-native animals, plants or microorganisms that enter ecosystems beyond their historical range and establish themselves there.

They may be called :-
🔹 Invaders
🔹 Non-natives
🔹 Exotics
🔹 Nuisance species

⭐ They often become strong competitors and can expand their geographic range rapidly.

title: 🌡️ 6.1.4.1 CAUSES OF INVASIVE SPECIES EXPANSION
notes:
Major factors include :-

🌡️ Climate change
🌊 Flooding
🚜 Land disturbance
🔥 Fire
🌾 Plowing
🚢 Transportation and shipping
🌍 Movement beyond natural geographic ranges

⭐ Disturbed environments often provide opportunities for invasive species to establish and spread.

title: 🌿 6.1.4.2 TERRESTRIAL INVASIVE SPECIES
notes:
Terrestrial invasive species occur mainly on land.

🌱 Phenotypic plasticity :- ability of an organism to change its characteristics in response to environmental conditions without necessarily involving permanent genetic change.

Example :- Purple loosestrife (Lythrum salicaria) can respond physically to different environmental conditions.

⭐ Invasive terrestrial plants can compete strongly with native vegetation for resources.

title: 💧 6.1.4.3 AQUATIC INVASIVE SPECIES
notes:
Aquatic invasive species live in water or wetland environments and can multiply rapidly.

Three major categories :-
🌊 Floating weeds :- rest on the water surface.
🌿 Emergent plants :- rooted in wet soil with parts growing above the water.
🌱 Submerged weeds :- grow mainly below the water surface.

⚠️ Impacts :-
🔹 Reduce freshwater quality
🔹 Compete for sunlight, nutrients and water
🔹 Reduce native biodiversity
🔹 Overgrow wetlands
🔹 Disrupt aquatic ecosystems

title: 🌿 6.1.4.4 WATER HYACINTH
notes:
Water hyacinth (Eichhornia crassipes) is an invasive aquatic plant.

📍 Originally native to South America.
🌊 Common in freshwater bodies, including Lake Tana.

⚠️ Effects :-
🔹 Forms dense growths
🔹 Reduces oxygen in water
🔹 Can kill fish populations
🔹 Reduces food supplies
🔹 Reduces local income
🔹 Disrupts aquatic ecosystems

⭐ Early prevention is cheaper and more effective than controlling widespread invasion.

title: 🔄 6.1.4.5 FOUR PHASES OF INVASIVE PLANT INVASION
notes:
1️⃣ Introduction :- invasive species arrive beyond their previous geographic range.

2️⃣ Naturalization :- the species establishes self-sustaining populations and spreads.

3️⃣ Colonization :- the founding population reproduces and forms a self-sustaining colony.

4️⃣ Dispersal :- the species spreads and establishes populations in new areas.

⭐ Management principle :- prevention is cheapest when the species is absent; once widespread, long-term control becomes much more expensive.

title: ⚠️ 6.1.4.6 IMPACTS OF INVASIVE SPECIES
notes:
Major impacts include :-

🌿 Biodiversity loss
🦋 Loss of native species
🐦 Loss of habitat and food for native animals
🔗 Disruption of pollination and seed dispersal
🌱 Disruption of plant succession
💧 Damage to freshwater ecosystems
🐟 Decline of fish populations
👥 Possible human-health impacts

⭐ Invasive species are an important driver of ecosystem degradation and species extinction.

title: 💰 6.2 POVERTY–ENVIRONMENT NEXUS
notes:
Poverty–environment nexus :- the mutually reinforcing relationship between poverty and environmental degradation.

🔄 Vicious cycle :-
Poverty → overuse of natural resources → environmental degradation → lower productivity and fewer resources → deeper poverty.

⭐ The relationship varies according to geographic, economic, social and cultural conditions.

🎯 Goal :- reduce poverty while protecting environmental resources.

title: 🏜️ 6.2.1 POVERTY AND LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
Land degradation :- persistent decline in land conditions resulting in reduced biodiversity, ecosystem functions, productivity and human values.

Major components :-
🌱 Soil degradation
🌿 Biological degradation
🌳 Vegetation changes
💧 Water-resource degradation

Causes of soil degradation include :-
🔹 Water erosion
🔹 Overcropping
🔹 Pollution
🔹 Salt deposition
🔹 Excessive chemical fertilizers
🔹 Loss of vegetation cover
🔹 Overgrazing

title: 🔄 6.2.1.1 VICIOUS CYCLE OF LAND DEGRADATION
notes:
Poor households may depend heavily on land and natural resources for their livelihoods.

🔄 Cycle :-
Low income → intensive resource use → land degradation → lower productivity → reduced income → greater poverty → further resource pressure.

⭐ Climate change can both contribute to land degradation and be affected by it.

title: 🛠️ 6.2.1.2 LAND DEGRADATION MANAGEMENT
notes:
🌱 Soil management :- control runoff, soil erosion, pH problems, salinization and compaction.

🌳 Vegetation management :- prevent overgrazing, improve cropland management, reduce forest loss and maintain tree diversity.

💧 Water management :- prevent over-extraction, protect aquifers and surface water, and manage floods and landslides.

🌍 Integrated management :- address biodiversity loss, dust storms, invasive species, pollution, urbanization, wetlands and wildlife corridors.

title: 🌳 6.2.2 POVERTY AND DEFORESTATION
notes:
Deforestation :- conversion of forest land into non-forest land.

🔗 Relationship with poverty is complex :-
🔹 Poor people may clear forests for survival.
🔹 Wealthier groups can also cause deforestation.
🔹 Deforestation can destroy resources used by poor households.
🔹 In some cases, forest exploitation can temporarily create income or assets.

⚠️ Long-term forest loss can reduce access to forest goods and environmental services.

title: 🌲 6.2.2.1 FOREST STRATEGIES FOR POVERTY REDUCTION
notes:
Three interdependent strategies :-

1️⃣ Strengthen the rights of local and marginalized groups and involve them in forest management.

2️⃣ Promote sustainable forestry, community forestry and agroforestry.

3️⃣ Integrate forests into sustainable economic development through better governance, legal reforms and investment.

4️⃣ Protect environmental values through protected areas, improved forest management and support for biodiversity and carbon sequestration.

title: 🌍 6.3 ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION AND SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
notes:
Environmental degradation :- deterioration of the environment through ecosystem destruction, habitat destruction, wildlife extinction, pollution and depletion of air, water and soil resources.

⭐ It threatens both environmental quality and human well-being.

🎯 Sustainable development seeks to meet human needs while maintaining the environmental systems needed by present and future generations.

title: 🌱 6.3.1 TYPES OF ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION
notes:
🌱 Soil degradation :- decline in soil quality caused by poor farming practices and excessive fertilizers and pesticides.

💧 Water degradation :- decline in water quality caused by waste, illegal dumping and industrial pollution.

🌬️ Atmospheric degradation :- deterioration of air quality, particle pollution and ozone-layer depletion.

🔊 Other pollution :- includes noise and light pollution.

title: ⚠️ 6.3.2 CAUSES OF ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION
notes:
Major causes include :-

🏗️ Land disturbance
🏭 Pollution
👥 Rapid population growth
🌾 Unsustainable agriculture
🌳 Deforestation
⛏️ Resource overexploitation
🏙️ Urbanization
🔥 Excessive consumption
🛢️ Fossil-fuel dependence

⭐ Rapid population growth can increase demand for food, materials, housing and energy, increasing pressure on land and natural resources.

title: 💥 6.3.3 EFFECTS OF ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION
notes:
Environmental degradation can cause :-

🌱 Soil fertility loss
💧 Water pollution
🌬️ Air pollution
🌳 Forest loss
🐾 Biodiversity loss
🦠 Species extinction
🍚 Food shortages
💧 Water scarcity
🏜️ Land degradation
🌡️ Climate-related problems
👥 Health problems
💰 Poverty and livelihood losses

⭐ Environmental degradation can therefore become both an ecological and socioeconomic problem.

title: ♻️ 6.3.4 ENVIRONMENTAL SUSTAINABILITY
notes:
Environmental sustainability :- maintaining essential ecological processes and life-support systems while conserving biodiversity and using species and ecosystems sustainably.

Important ecological processes include :-
🌱 Soil regeneration
♻️ Nutrient recycling
💧 Water purification
🧬 Genetic diversity
🌿 Ecosystem functioning

⭐ Sustainable resource use protects the ecological foundations of human survival and development.

title: 🌍 6.3.5 SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT
notes:
Sustainable development requires balancing environmental protection with human well-being and economic development.

Important principles :-
🌱 Preserve Earth's vitality and diversity.
👥 Improve human well-being.
⛏️ Reduce depletion of non-renewable resources.
♻️ Promote responsible resource use.
🌳 Protect ecosystems.
📚 Increase environmental awareness.

⭐ Sustainable development connects environmental protection with long-term socioeconomic development.

title: 🛡️ 6.3.6 MEASURES TO REDUCE ENVIRONMENTAL DEGRADATION
notes:
Important measures include :-

🌳 Stop deforestation.
🏛️ Strengthen government environmental regulations.
🚯 Control illegal dumping.
♻️ Recycle and reuse materials.
🗑️ Reduce waste.
🚫 Reduce plastic pollution.
🌱 Promote sustainable agriculture.
💧 Conserve water.
⚡ Increase renewable-energy use.
📚 Promote environmental education.
🤝 Encourage community participation.

⭐ Adaptation, conservation and responsible resource management are essential for long-term sustainability.

title: 🧠 UNIT 6 KEY CONCEPTS
notes:
🏞️ Habitat :- environmental conditions that allow a species to survive and reproduce.

🧩 Habitat fragmentation :- breaking a continuous habitat into smaller separated areas.

⏳ Extinction debt :- delay between habitat change and eventual species extinction.

🌾 Agricultural intensification :- increasing agricultural output per unit of input.

🐟 Overfishing :- fishing stocks below the level required for long-term sustainable yield.

🐄 Overgrazing :- grazing beyond the carrying capacity of land.

🌳 Over-logging :- cutting forests faster than regeneration.

💧 Over-drafting :- extracting groundwater faster than recharge.

🦠 Invasive alien species :- non-native organisms that establish and spread beyond their historical range.

🌊 Floating weeds :- aquatic plants that rest on the water surface.

🌿 Emergent plants :- aquatic plants rooted in wet soil with parts above water.

🌱 Submerged weeds :- aquatic plants growing mainly beneath the water surface.

💰 Poverty–environment nexus :- mutually reinforcing relationship between poverty and environmental degradation.

🏜️ Land degradation :- persistent decline in land condition and productivity.

🌳 Deforestation :- conversion of forest to non-forest land.

🌍 Environmental degradation :- deterioration of environmental quality through ecosystem destruction, pollution and resource depletion.

♻️ Environmental sustainability :- maintaining ecological processes, biodiversity and sustainable resource use.

🌱 Sustainable development :- development that balances human well-being, economic needs and environmental protection.

title: ⭐ UNIT 6 QUICK REVISION
notes:
📌 Persistent environmental changes include habitat destruction, agricultural intensification, resource overexploitation and invasive species.

📌 Human landscape modification is a major cause of habitat loss and fragmentation.

📌 Habitat destruction reduces biodiversity and can eventually lead to species extinction.

📌 Extinction debt is the time between landscape change and eventual extinction.

📌 Agricultural intensification increases output but can cause biodiversity loss, soil degradation, pesticide hazards, water pollution and soil compaction.

📌 Sustainable intensification combines higher productivity with soil, water, pest and biodiversity management.

📌 Overexploitation occurs when resource extraction exceeds regeneration.

📌 Major forms include overfishing, overgrazing, over-logging and over-drafting.

📌 Invasive alien species can rapidly spread into ecosystems beyond their historical range.

📌 Aquatic invasive plants are classified as floating, emergent and submerged.

📌 Water hyacinth can reduce oxygen, kill fish and reduce local income and food supply.

📌 The four invasion phases are introduction → naturalization → colonization → dispersal.

📌 Prevention is cheaper and more effective before invasive species become widespread.

📌 Poverty and environmental degradation form a vicious cycle: poverty can increase resource pressure, while degradation can deepen poverty.

📌 Land degradation includes soil, biological, vegetation and water-resource degradation.

📌 Deforestation is closely connected with poverty because forests provide important goods and services to poor households.

📌 Environmental degradation includes soil, water, atmospheric, noise and light degradation.

📌 Major causes include land disturbance, pollution, rapid population growth, deforestation and overexploitation.

📌 Environmental sustainability protects ecological processes, biodiversity and natural resources.

📌 Sustainable development requires a balance between environmental preservation, human well-being and economic development.

⭐ Core idea :- Human activities can permanently damage ecosystems and resources, but sustainable agriculture, conservation, responsible resource use, poverty reduction and environmental protection can help maintain Earth's ecological systems.
